entries.b7eebd93064782f3cbacbb74b6f65c523991c2b6: <div sID="gen8445" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="32" osisID="2Chr.32" sID="2Chr.32"/> <div eID="gen8445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8446" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8447" type="x-p"/> This chapter continues and concludes the history of the reign of Hezekiah. I. The descent which Sennacherib made upon him, and the care he took to fortify himself, his city, and the minds of his people, against that enemy, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.1-2Chr.32.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. The insolent blasphemous letters and messages which Sennacherib sent him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.9-2Chr.32.19">ver. 9-19</reference>. III. The real answer God gave to Sennacherib's blasphemies, and to Hezekiah's prayers, in the total rout of the Assyrian army, to the shame of Sennacherib and the honour of Hezekiah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.20-2Chr.32.23">ver. 20-23</reference>. IV. Hezekiah's sickness and his recovery from that, his sin and his recovery from that, with the honours that attended him living and dead, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.24-2Chr.32.33">ver. 24-33</reference>.
entries.7f4eee1a88a8c5ee82e080a64f4d1d2c4fff29cc: <div eID="gen8447" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8446" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Sennacherib's Invasion; Hezekiah's Patient Confidence. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 713.)</title> <div sID="gen8448" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> After these things, and the establishment thereof, Sennacherib king of Assyria came, and entered into Judah, and encamped against the fenced cities, and thought to win them for himself. <hi type="super">2</hi> And when Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib was come, and that he was purposed to fight against Jerusalem, <hi type="super">3</hi> He took counsel with his princes and his mighty men to stop the waters of the fountains which <hi type="italic">were</hi> without the city: and they did help him. <hi type="super">4</hi> So there was gathered much people together, who stopped all the fountains, and the brook that ran through the midst of the land, saying, Why should the kings of Assyria come, and find much water? <hi type="super">5</hi> Also he strengthened himself, and built up all the wall that was broken, and raised <hi type="italic">it</hi> up to the towers, and another wall without, and repaired Millo <hi type="italic">in</hi> the city of David, and made darts and shields in abundance. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he set captains of war over the people, and gathered them together to him in the street of the gate of the city, and spake comfortably to them, saying, <hi type="super">7</hi> Be strong and courageous, be not afraid nor dismayed for the king of Assyria, nor for all the multitude that <hi type="italic">is</hi> with him: for <hi type="italic">there be</hi> more with us than with him: <hi type="super">8</hi> With him <hi type="italic">is</hi> an arm of flesh; but with us <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God to help us, and to fight our battles. And the people rested themselves upon the words of Hezekiah king of Judah. <div eID="gen8448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8449" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The formidable design of Sennacherib against Hezekiah's kingdom, and the vigorous attempt he made upon it. This Sennacherib was now, as Nebuchadnezzar was afterwards, the terror and scourge and great oppressor of that part of the world. He aimed to raise a boundless monarchy for himself upon the ruins of all his neighbours. His predecessor Shalmaneser had lately made himself master of the kingdom of Israel, and carried the ten tribes captives. Sennacherib thought, in like manner, to win Judah for himself. Pride and ambition put men upon grasping at universal dominion. It is observable that, just about this time, Rome, a city which afterwards came to reign more than any other had done <hi type="italic">over the kings of the earth,</hi> was built by Romulus. Sennacherib invaded Judah immediately after the reformation of it and the re-establishment of religion in it: <hi type="italic">After these things he entered into Judah,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.1">v. 1</reference>. 1. It was well ordered by the divine Providence that he did not give them this disturbance before the reformation was finished and established, as it might then have put a stop to it. 2. Perhaps he intended to chastise Hezekiah for destroying that idolatry to which he himself was devoted. He looked upon Hezekiah as profane in what he had done, and as having thrown himself out of the divine protection. He accordingly considered him as one who might easily be made a prey of. 3. God ordered it at this time that he might have an opportunity of showing himself strong on the behalf of this returning reforming people. He brought this trouble upon them that he might have the honour, and might put on them the honour, of their deliverance. <hi type="italic">After these things, and the establishment thereof,</hi> one would have expected to hear of nothing but perfect peace, and that none durst meddle with a people thus qualified for the divine favour; yet the next news we hear is that a threatening destroying army enters the country, and is ready to lay all waste. We may be in the way of our duty and yet meet with trouble and danger. God orders it so for the trial of our confidence in him and the manifestation of his care concerning us. The little opposition which Sennacherib met with in entering Judah induced him to imagine that all was his own. He thought to <hi type="italic">win all the fenced cities</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.1">v. 1</reference>), and purposed to <hi type="italic">fight against Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.2">v. 2</reference>. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.7">2 Kings xviii. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.13">13</reference>. <div eID="gen8449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8450" type="x-p"/> II. The preparation which Hezekiah prudently made against this storm that threatened him: <hi type="italic">He took counsel with his princes</hi> what he should do, what measures he should take, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.3">v. 3</reference>. With their advice he provided, 1. That the country should give him a cold reception, for he took care that he should find no water in it (and then his army must perish for thirst), or at least that there should be a scarcity of water, by which his army would be weakened and unfitted for service. A powerful army, if it want water but a few days, will be but a heap of dry dust. All hands were set immediately to work to <hi type="italic">stop up the fountains,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the brook that ran through the midst of the land,</hi> turning that (it is probable) into the city by pipes under-ground. Such as this is the policy commonly practised now-a-days of destroying the forage before an invading army. 2. That the city should give him a warm reception. In order to this he repaired the wall, raised towers, and made darts (or, as it is in the margin, <hi type="italic">swords</hi> or <hi type="italic">weapons</hi>) and shields in abundance (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.5">v. 5</reference>), and appointed captains, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.6">v. 6</reference>. Note, Those that trust God with their safety must yet use proper means for their safety, otherwise they tempt him, and do not trust him. <hi type="italic">God will provide,</hi> but so must we also. <div eID="gen8450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8451" type="x-p"/> III. The encouragement which he gave to his people to depend upon God in this distress. He gathered them together in a broad open street, and <hi type="italic">spoke comfortably to them,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.6">v. 6</reference>. He was himself undaunted, being confident the invasion would issue well. He was not like his father, who had much guilt to terrify him and no faith to encourage him, so that, in a time of public danger, <hi type="italic">his heart was moved, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind,</hi> and then no marvel that <hi type="italic">the heart of his people was so too,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.7.2">Isa. vii. 2</reference>. With what he said he put life into his people, his captains especially, and <hi type="italic">spoke to their heart,</hi> as the word is. 1. He endeavoured to keep down their fears: "<hi type="italic">Be strong and courageous;</hi> do not think of surrendering the city or capitulating, but resolve to hold it out to the last man; do not think of losing the city, nor of falling into the enemy's hand; there is no danger. Let the soldiers be bold and brave, make good their posts, stand to their arms, and fight manfully, and let the citizens encourage them to do so: <hi type="italic">Be not afraid nor dismayed for the king of Assyria.</hi>" The prophet had thus encouraged them from God (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.24">Isa. x. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Be not afraid of the Assyrians;</hi> and here the king from him. Now it was that <hi type="italic">the sinners in Zion were afraid</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">Isa. xxxiii. 14</reference>), but the righteous <hi type="italic">dwelt on high</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.15-Isa.33.16">Isa. xxxiii. 15, 16</reference>) and <hi type="italic">meditated on terror</hi> so as to conquer it. See <reference osisRef="Isa.33.18">Isa. xxxiii. 18</reference>, which refers to what is recorded here. 2. He endeavoured to keep up their faith, in order to the silencing and suppressing of their fears. "Sennacherib has a <hi type="italic">multitude with him,</hi> and yet there are <hi type="italic">more with us than with him;</hi> for we have God with us, and how many do you reckon him for? With our enemy is an arm of flesh, which he trusts to; but <hi type="italic">with us is the Lord,</hi> whose power is irresistible, our God, whose promise is inviolable, a God in covenant with us, <hi type="italic">to help us, and to fight our battles,</hi> not only to help us to fight them, but to fight them for us if he please:" and so he did here. Note, A believing confidence in God will raise us above the prevailing fear of man. He that <hi type="italic">feareth the fury of the oppressor forgetteth the Lord his Maker,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12-Isa.51.13">Isa. li. 12, 13</reference>. It is probable that Hezekiah said more to this purport, and that the people rested themselves upon what he said, not merely upon his word, but on the things he said concerning the presence of God with them and his power to relieve them, the belief of which made them easy. Let the good subjects and soldiers of Jesus Christ rest thus upon his word, and boldly say, <hi type="italic">Since God is for us, who can be against us?</hi>
entries.e59ee62c9b89d570c64390969993edc5f86f2379: <div eID="gen8451" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Destruction of the Assyrians. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 713.)</title> <div sID="gen8452" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> After this did Sennacherib king of Assyria send his servants to Jerusalem, (but he <hi type="italic">himself laid siege</hi> against Lachish, and all his power with him,) unto Hezekiah king of Judah, and unto all Judah that <hi type="italic">were</hi> at Jerusalem, saying, <hi type="super">10</hi> Thus saith Sennacherib king of Assyria, Whereon do ye trust, that ye abide in the siege in Jerusalem? <hi type="super">11</hi> Doth not Hezekiah persuade you to give over yourselves to die by famine and by thirst, saying, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God shall deliver us out of the hand of the king of Assyria? <hi type="super">12</hi> Hath not the same Hezekiah taken away his high places and his altars, and commanded Judah and Jerusalem, saying, Ye shall worship before one altar, and burn incense upon it? <hi type="super">13</hi> Know ye not what I and my fathers have done unto all the people of <hi type="italic">other</hi> lands? were the gods of the nations of those lands any ways able to deliver their lands out of mine hand? <hi type="super">14</hi> Who <hi type="italic">was there</hi> among all the gods of those nations that my fathers utterly destroyed, that could deliver his people out of mine hand, that your God should be able to deliver you out of mine hand? <hi type="super">15</hi> Now therefore let not Hezekiah deceive you, nor persuade you on this manner, neither yet believe him: for no god of any nation or kingdom was able to deliver his people out of mine hand, and out of the hand of my fathers: how much less shall your God deliver you out of mine hand? <hi type="super">16</hi> And his servants spake yet <hi type="italic">more</hi> against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God, and against his servant Hezekiah. <hi type="super">17</hi> He wrote also letters to rail on the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, and to speak against him, saying, As the gods of the nations of <hi type="italic">other</hi> lands have not delivered their people out of mine hand, so shall not the God of Hezekiah deliver his people out of mine hand. <hi type="super">18</hi> Then they cried with a loud voice in the Jews' speech unto the people of Jerusalem that <hi type="italic">were</hi> on the wall, to affright them, and to trouble them; that they might take the city. <hi type="super">19</hi> And they spake against the God of Jerusalem, as against the gods of the people of the earth, <hi type="italic">which were</hi> the work of the hands of man. <hi type="super">20</hi> And for this <hi type="italic">cause</hi> Hezekiah the king, and the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz, prayed and cried to heaven. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sent an angel, which cut off all the mighty men of valour, and the leaders and captains in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he returned with shame of face to his own land. And when he was come into the house of his god, they that came forth of his own bowels slew him there with the sword. <hi type="super">22</hi> Thus the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib the king of Assyria, and from the hand of all <hi type="italic">other,</hi> and guided them on every side. <hi type="super">23</hi> And many brought gifts unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to Jerusalem, and presents to Hezekiah king of Judah: so that he was magnified in the sight of all nations from thenceforth. <div eID="gen8452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8453" type="x-p"/> This story of the rage and blasphemy of Sennacherib, Hezekiah's prayer, and the deliverance of Jerusalem by the destruction of the Assyrian army, we had more at large in the book of Kings, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.1-2Kgs.19.37">2 Kings xviii. and xix.</reference> It is contracted here, yet large enough to show these three things:— <div eID="gen8453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8454" type="x-p"/> I. The impiety and malice of the church's enemies. Sennacherib has his hands full in besieging Lachish (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.9">v. 9</reference>), but hears that Hezekiah is fortifying Jerusalem and encouraging his people to stand it out; and therefore, before he come in person to besiege it, he sends messengers to make speeches, and he himself writes letters to frighten Hezekiah and his people into a surrender of the city. See, 1. His great malice against the king of Judah, in endeavouring to withdraw his subjects from their allegiance to him. He did not treat with Hezekiah as a man of honour would have done, nor propose fair terms to him, but used mean and base artifices, unbecoming a crowned head, to terrify the common people and persuade them to desert him. He represented Hezekiah as one who designed to deceive his subjects into their ruin and betray them <hi type="italic">to famine and thirst</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.11">v. 11</reference>), as one who had done them great wrong and exposed them already to the divine displeasure by taking away the high places and altars (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.12">v. 12</reference>), and who, against the common interest of his people, held out against a force that would certainly be their ruin, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.15">v. 15</reference>. 2. His great impiety against the God of Israel, <hi type="italic">the God of Jerusalem</hi> he is called (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.19">v. 19</reference>), because that was the place he had chosen to put his name there, and because that was the place which was now threatened by the enemy and which the divine Providence had under its special protection. This proud blasphemer compared the great Jehovah, the Maker of heaven and earth, with the dunghill gods of the nations, the work of men's hands, and thought him no more able to deliver his worshippers than they were to deliver theirs (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.19">v. 19</reference>), as if an infinite and eternal Spirit had no more wisdom and power than a stone or the stock of a tree. He boasted of his triumphs over the gods of the nations, that they could none of them protect their people (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.13-2Chr.32.15">v. 13-15</reference>), and thence inferred not only, <hi type="italic">How shall your God deliver you?</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.14">v. 14</reference>), but, as if he were inferior to them all, <hi type="italic">How much less shall your God deliver you?</hi> as if he were less able to help than any of them. Thus did they rail, rail in writing (which, being more deliberate, is so much the worse), <hi type="italic">on the Lord God of Israel,</hi> as if he were a cipher and an empty name, like all the rest, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.17">v. 17</reference>. Sennacherib, in the instructions he gave, said more than enough; but, as if his blasphemies had been too little, his servants, who learned insolence from their master, spoke yet more than he bade them <hi type="italic">against the Lord God and his servant Hezekiah,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.16">v. 16</reference>. And God resents what is said against his servants, and will reckon for it, as well as what is said against himself. All this was intended to frighten the people from their hope in God, which David's enemies sought to take him off from (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.1">Ps. xi. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.42.10">xlii. 10</reference>), saying, <hi type="italic">There is no help for him in God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.3.2">Ps. iii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.71.11">lxxi. 11</reference>. Thus they hoped to take the city by weakening the hands of those that should defend it. Satan, in his temptations, aims to destroy our faith in God's all-sufficiency, knowing that he shall gain his point if he can do that; as we keep our ground if our <hi type="italic">faith fail not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.22.32">Luke xxii. 32</reference>. <div eID="gen8454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8455" type="x-p"/> II. The duty as well as the interest of the church's friends, and that is in the day of distress to pray and cry to Heaven. So Hezekiah did, and the prophet Isaiah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.20">v. 20</reference>. It was a happy time when the king and the prophet joined thus in prayer. Is any troubled? Is any terrified? Let him pray. So we engage God for us; so we encourage ourselves in him. Praying to God is here called <hi type="italic">crying to Heaven,</hi> because we are, in prayer, to eye him as our Father in heaven, whence he beholds the children of men, and where he has prepared his throne. <div eID="gen8455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8456" type="x-p"/> III. The power and goodness of the church's God. He is able both to control his enemies, be they ever so high, and to relieve his friends, be they ever so low. <div eID="gen8456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8457" type="x-p"/> 1. As the blasphemies of his enemies engage him against them (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.27">Deut. xxxii. 27</reference>), so the prayers of his people engage him for them. They did so here. (1.) The army of the Assyrians was cut off by the sword of an angel, which triumphed particularly in the slaughter of the mighty men of valour, and the leaders and captains, who defied the sword of any man. God delights to abase the proud and secure. The Targum says, The Word of the Lord (the eternal Word) sent Gabriel to do this execution, and that it was done with lightning, and in the passover night: that was the night in which the angel destroyed the first-born of Egypt. But that was not all. (2.) The king of the Assyrians, having received this disgrace, was cut off by the sword of his own sons. Those that <hi type="italic">came forth of his own bowels slew him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.21">v. 21</reference>. Thus was he mortified first, and then murdered—shamed first, and then slain. Evil pursues sinners; and, when they escape one mischief, they run upon another unseen. <div eID="gen8457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8458" type="x-p"/> 2. By this work of wonder, (1.) God was glorified, as the protector of his people. Thus he saved Jerusalem, not only from the hand of Sennacherib, but from the hand <hi type="italic">of all others,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.22">v. 22</reference>; for such a deliverance as this was an earnest of much mercy in store; and he <hi type="italic">guided them,</hi> that is, he guarded them, on every side. God defends his people by directing them, shows them what they should do, and so saves them from what is designed or done against them. For this <hi type="italic">many brought gifts unto the Lord,</hi> when they saw the great power of God in the defence of his people. Strangers were thereby induced to supplicate his favour and enemies to deprecate his wrath, and both brought gifts to his temple, in token of their care and desire. (2.) Hezekiah was magnified as the favourite and particular care of Heaven. Many <hi type="italic">brought presents to him</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.22-2Chr.32.23">v. 22, 23</reference>), in token of the honour they had for him, and to make an interest in him. By the favour of God enemies are lost and friends gained.
entries.599c3abbea067e634f95035d1bd9e7127c295cfc: <div eID="gen8458" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Death of Hezekiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 698.)</title> <div sID="gen8459" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> In those days Hezekiah was sick to the death, and prayed unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and he spake unto him, and he gave him a sign. <hi type="super">25</hi> But Hezekiah rendered not again according to the benefit <hi type="italic">done</hi> unto him; for his heart was lifted up: therefore there was wrath upon him, and upon Judah and Jerusalem. <hi type="super">26</hi> Notwithstanding Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, <hi type="italic">both</hi> he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came not upon them in the days of Hezekiah. <hi type="super">27</hi> And Hezekiah had exceeding much riches and honour: and he made himself treasuries for silver, and for gold, and for precious stones, and for spices, and for shields, and for all manner of pleasant jewels; <hi type="super">28</hi> Storehouses also for the increase of corn, and wine, and oil; and stalls for all manner of beasts, and cotes for flocks. <hi type="super">29</hi> Moreover he provided him cities, and possessions of flocks and herds in abundance: for God had given him substance very much. <hi type="super">30</hi> This same Hezekiah also stopped the upper watercourse of Gihon, and brought it straight down to the west side of the city of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all his works. <hi type="super">31</hi> Howbeit in <hi type="italic">the business of</hi> the ambassadors of the princes of Babylon, who sent unto him to enquire of the wonder that was <hi type="italic">done</hi> in the land, God left him, to try him, that he might know all <hi type="italic">that was</hi> in his heart. <hi type="super">32</hi> Now the rest of the acts of Hezekiah, and his goodness, behold, they <hi type="italic">are</hi> written in the vision of Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, <hi type="italic">and</hi> in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel. <hi type="super">33</hi> And Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the chiefest of the sepulchres of the sons of David: and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem did him honour at his death. And Manasseh his son reigned in his stead. <div eID="gen8459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8460" type="x-p"/> Here we conclude the story of Hezekiah with an account of three things concerning him:— <div eID="gen8460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8461" type="x-p"/> I. His sickness and his recovery from it, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.24">v. 24</reference>. The account of his sickness is but briefly mentioned here; we had a large narrative of it, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.1-2Kgs.20.11">2 Kings xx.</reference> His disease seemed likely to be mortal. In the extremity of it he prayed. God answered him, and gave him a sign that he should recover, the going back of the sun ten degrees. <div eID="gen8461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8462" type="x-p"/> II. His sin and his repentance for it, which were also more largely related, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.12-2Kgs.20.21">2 Kings xx. 12</reference>, &c. Yet several things are here observed concerning his sin which we had not there. 1. The occasion of it was the king of Babylon's sending an honourable embassy to him to congratulate him on his recovery. But here it is added that they came to enquire of <hi type="italic">the wonder that was done in the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.31">v. 31</reference>), either the destruction of the Assyrian army or the going back of the sun. The Assyrians were their enemies; they came to enquire concerning their fall, that they might triumph in it. The sun was their god; they came to enquire concerning the favour he had shown to Hezekiah, that they might honour him whom their god honoured, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.31">v. 31</reference>. These miracles were wrought to alarm and awaken a stupid careless world, and turn them from dumb and lame idols to the living God; and men were startled by them, but not converted till a greater wonder was done in that land, in the appearing of Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="Matt.2.1-Matt.2.2">Matt. ii. 1, 2</reference>. 2. God left him to himself in it, to try him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.31">v. 31</reference>. God, by the power of his almighty grace, could have prevented the sin; but he permitted it for wise and holy ends, that, by this trial and his weakness in it, he might know, that is, it might be known (a usual Hebraism), what was in his heart, that he was not so perfect in grace as he thought he was, but had his follies and infirmities as other men. God left him to himself to be proud of his wealth, to keep him from being proud of his holiness. It is good for us to know ourselves, and our own weakness and sinfulness, that we may not be conceited or self-confident, but may always think meanly of ourselves and live in a dependence upon divine grace. We know not the corruption of our own hearts, nor what we shall do if God leave us to ourselves. <hi type="italic">Lord, lead us not into temptation.</hi> 3. His sin was that <hi type="italic">his heart was lifted up,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.25">v. 25</reference>. He was proud of the honour God had put upon him in so many instances, the honour his neighbours did him in bringing him presents, and now that the king of Babylon should send an embassy to him to caress and court him: this exalted him above measure. When Hezekiah had destroyed other idolatries he began to idolize himself. O what need have great men, and good men, and useful men, to study their own infirmities and follies, and their obligations to free grace, that they may never think highly of themselves, and to beg earnestly of God that he will hide pride from them and always keep them humble! 4. The aggravation of his sin was that he made so bad a return to God for his favours to him, making even those favours the food and fuel of his pride (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">He rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him.</hi> Note, It is justly expected that those who have received mercy from God should study to make some suitable returns for the mercies they have received; and, if they do not, their ingratitude will certainly be charged upon them. Though we cannot render an equivalent, or the payment of a debt, we must render the acknowledgment of a favour. <hi type="italic">What shall I render</hi> that may be so accepted? <reference osisRef="Ps.116.12">Ps. cxvi. 12</reference>. 5. The divine displeasure he was under for this sin; though it was but a heart-sin, and the overt-act seemed not only innocent but civil (the showing of his treasures to a friend), yet wrath came upon him and his kingdom for it, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.25">v. 25</reference>. Note, Pride is a sin that God hates as much as any, and particularly in his own people. Those that exalt themselves must expect to be abased, and put under humbling providences. Wrath came on David for his pride in numbering the people. 6. His repentance for this sin: <hi type="italic">He humbled himself for the pride of his heart.</hi> Note, (1.) Though God may, for wise and holy ends, suffer his people to fall into sin, yet he will not suffer them to lie still in it; they <hi type="italic">shall not be utterly cast down.</hi> (2.) Heart-sins are to be repented of, though they go no further. (3.) Self-humiliation is a necessary branch of repentance. (4.) Pride of heart, by which we have lifted up ourselves, is a sin for which we ought in a special manner to humble ourselves. (5.) People ought to mourn for the sins of their rulers. The inhabitants of Jerusalem humbled themselves with Hezekiah, because they either knew that they also had been guilty of the same sin, or at least feared that they might share in the punishment. When David, in his pride, numbered the people, they all smarted for his sin. 7. The reprieve granted thereupon. The wrath came not in his days. While he lived the country had peace and truth prevailed; so much does repentance avail to put by, or at least to put off, the tokens of God's anger. <div eID="gen8462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8463" type="x-p"/> III. Here is the honour done to Hezekiah, 1. By the providence of God while he lived. He had <hi type="italic">exceeding much riches and honour</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.27">v. 27</reference>), replenished his stores, victualled his campus, fortified his city, and did all he wished to do; for God <hi type="italic">had given him very much substance,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.29">v. 29</reference>. Among his great performances, his turning the water-course of Gihon is mentioned (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.30">v. 30</reference>), which was done upon occasion of Sennacherib's invasion, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.3-2Chr.32.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. The water had come into that which is called the <hi type="italic">old pool</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa. xxii. 11</reference>) and the <hi type="italic">upper pool</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.3">Isa. vii. 3</reference>); but he gathered the waters into a new place, for the greater convenience of the city, called the <hi type="italic">lower pool,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.22.9">Isa. xxii. 9</reference>. And, in general, he <hi type="italic">prospered in all his works,</hi> for they were good works. 2. By the respect paid to his memory when he was dead. (1.) The prophet Isaiah wrote his life and reign (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.32">v. 32</reference>), his acts and his goodness or piety, or which it is part of the honour to be recorded and remembered, for examples to others. (2.) The people <hi type="italic">did him honour at his death</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.33">v. 33</reference>), buried him in the chief of the sepulchres, made as great a burning for him as for Asa, or, which is a much greater honour, made great lamentation for him, as for Josiah. See how the honour of serious godliness is manifested in the consciences of men. Though it is to be feared that the generality of the people did not heartily comply with the reforming kings, yet they could not but praise their endeavours for reformation, and the memory of those kings was blessed among them. It is a debt we owe to those who have been eminently useful in their day to do them honour at their death, when they are out of the reach of flattery and we have seen the end of their conversation. The due payment of this debt will be an encouragement to others to do likewise.  <chapter eID="2Chr.32"/> <div eID="gen8463" type="x-p"/>

entries.67a95994652a2efc24f90709627c57f55a8192db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4158"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 32</title> <div sID="gen6036" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.1-2Chr.32.20">2Ch 32:1-20</reference>. Sennacherib Invades Judah.<div eID="gen6036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6037" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4158"/><hi type="bold">1. After these things, and the establishment thereof--</hi>that is, the restoration of the temple-worship. The precise date is given, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.13">2Ki 18:13</reference>. Determined to recover the independence of his country, Hezekiah had decided to refuse to pay the tribute which his father had bound himself to pay to Assyria.<div eID="gen6037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sennacherib ... entered into Judah, and encamped against the fenced cities--</hi>The whole land was ravaged; the strong fortresses of Ashdod (<reference osisRef="Isa.20.1">Is 20:1</reference>) and Lachish had fallen; the siege of Libnah had commenced, when the king of Judah, doubting his ability to resist, sent to acknowledge his fault, and offer terms of submission by paying the tribute. The commencement of this Assyrian war was disastrous to Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.13">2Ki 18:13</reference>). But the misfortunes of the early period of the war are here passed over, as the historian hastens to relate the remarkable deliverance which God wrought for His kingdom of Judah. <div eID="gen6038" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc730ee85d97617188f0bf9af5e49e702a94d18b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4159"/><div sID="gen6039" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4159"/><hi type="bold">2-8. when Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib ... was purposed to fight against Jerusalem--</hi>An account of the means taken to fortify Jerusalem against the threatened siege is given only in this passage. The polluting or filling up of wells, and the altering of the course of rivers, is an old practice that still obtains in the wars of the East. Hezekiah's plan was to cover the fountain heads, so that they might not be discovered by the enemy, and to carry the water by subterranean channels or pipes into the city--a plan which, while it would secure a constant supply to the inhabitants, would distress the besiegers, as the country all around Jerusalem was very destitute of water. <div eID="gen6039" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d5d3e80df91f26bf62541bf81dddba9554cd12a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4163"/><div sID="gen6043" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4163"/>9-20. (See on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.17-2Kgs.18.35">2Ki 18:17-35</reference>; also <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.8-2Kgs.19.34">2Ki 19:8-34</reference>). <div eID="gen6043" type="x-p"/>
entries.240bc1c501f701cde7bf8fa9d8f54039376c7af1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4165"/><div sID="gen6046" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4165"/><hi type="bold">21. an angel ... cut off all the mighty men--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35-2Kgs.19.37">2Ki 19:35-37</reference>).<div eID="gen6046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6047" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.24-2Chr.32.26">2Ch 32:24-26</reference>. Hezekiah's Sickness and Recovery. <div eID="gen6047" type="x-p"/>
entries.0428251e28aa12ffe229865c27407f8ab7fc099d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4166"/><div sID="gen6048" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4166"/><hi type="bold">24. In those days Hezekiah was sick to the death--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.1-2Kgs.20.11">2Ki 20:1-11</reference>).<div eID="gen6048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6049" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.27-2Chr.32.33">2Ch 32:27-33</reference>. His Riches and Works. <div eID="gen6049" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0d5fb9fa4c9b7f0607604c9c110b1830f812b5b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4167"/><div sID="gen6050" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4167"/><hi type="bold">27-29. he had exceeding much riches and honour--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.13">2Ki 20:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.39.2">Is 39:2</reference>). A great portion of his personal wealth, like that of David and Uzziah, consisted in immense possessions of agricultural and pastoral produce. Besides, he had accumulated large treasures in gold, silver, and precious things, which he had taken as spoils from the Philistines, and which he had received as presents from neighboring states, among which he was held in great honor as a king under the special protection of Heaven. Much of his great wealth he expended in improving his capital, erecting forts, and promoting the internal benefit of his kingdom. <div eID="gen6050" type="x-p"/>
entries.773233f450433f50a89d32cca4b9ebccf36e8c07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4168"/><div sID="gen6051" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4168"/><hi type="bold">30. stopped the ... watercourse of Gihon, and brought it ... to the west side of the city, &c.--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.20">2Ki 20:20</reference>). Particular notice is here taken of the aqueduct, as among the greatest of Hezekiah's works. "In exploring the subterranean channel conveying the water from Virgin's Fount to Siloam, I discovered a similar channel entering from the north, a few yards from its commencement; and on tracing it up near the Mugrabin gate, where it became so choked with rubbish that it could be traversed no farther, I there found it turn to the west in the direction of the south end of the cleft, or saddle, of Zion, and if this channel was not constructed for the purpose of conveying the waters of Hezekiah's aqueduct, I am unable to suggest any purpose to which it could have been applied. Perhaps the reason why it was not brought down on the Zion side, was that Zion was already well-watered in its lower portion by the Great Pool, 'the lower pool of Gihon.' And accordingly Williams [Holy City] renders this passage, 'He stopped the upper outflow of the waters of Gihon, and led them down westward to the city'" [Barclay, City of the Great King]. The construction of this aqueduct required not only masonic but engineering skill; for the passage was bored through a continuous mass of rock. Hezekiah's pool or reservoir made to receive the water within the northwest part of the city still remains. It is an oblong quadrangular tank, two hundred forty feet in length, from one hundred forty-four to one hundred fifty in breadth, but, from recent excavations, appears to have extended somewhat farther towards the north. <div eID="gen6051" type="x-p"/>
entries.729b63aabb9b1ebd56195afe3238688da3beec2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4169"/><div sID="gen6052" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4169"/><hi type="bold">31. in the business of the ambassadors who sent ... to inquire of the wonder that was done in the land, &c.--</hi>They brought a present (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.23">2Ch 32:23</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.12">2Ki 20:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.13">13</reference>), and a letter of congratulation on his recovery, in which particular enquiries were made about the miracle of the sun's retrocession--a natural phenomenon that could not fail to excite great interest and curiosity at Babylon, where astronomy was so much studied. At the same time, there is reason to believe that they proposed a defensive league against the Assyrians.<div eID="gen6052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God left him, to try him, &c.--</hi>Hezekiah's offense was not so much in the display of his military stores and treasures, as in not giving to God the glory both of the miracle and of his recovery, and thus leading those heathen ambassadors to know Him. <chapter eID="2Chr.32"/>

entries.5fbe1923efb63bfee8118781277686022c3fa624: <div eID="gen14568" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14569" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14570" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14570" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14569" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14571" type="x-p"/> Sennacherib invades Judea, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.1">2Chr 32:1</reference>. Hezekiah takes proper measures for the defense of his kingdom, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.2-2Chr.32.6">2Chr 32:2-6</reference>. His exhortation, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.7">2Chr 32:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.8">2Chr 32:8</reference>. Sennacherib sends a blasphemous message to Hezekiah, and to the people, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.9-2Chr.32.15">2Chr 32:9-15</reference>. His servants rail against God; and he and they blaspheme most grievously, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.16-2Chr.32.19">2Chr 32:16-19</reference>. Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah cry to God; he answers, and the Assyrians are destroyed, and Sennacherib is slain by his own sons, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.20">2Chr 32:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.21">2Chr 32:21</reference>. The Lord is magnified, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.22">2Chr 32:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.23">2Chr 32:23</reference>. Hezekiah's sickness and recovery, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.24">2Chr 32:24</reference>. His ingratitude, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.25">2Chr 32:25</reference>. His humiliation, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.26">2Chr 32:26</reference>. His riches, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.27-2Chr.32.30">2Chr 32:27-30</reference>. His error relative to the Babylonish ambassadors, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.31">2Chr 32:31</reference>. His acts and death, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.32">2Chr 32:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.33">2Chr 32:33</reference>. <div eID="gen14571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14572" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen14572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14573" type="x-p"/> After these things - God did not permit this pious prince to be disturbed till he had completed the reformation which he had begun.
entries.4e268ff13325f168b3743f836ab8e7d3b5e99354: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen14573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14574" type="x-p"/> When Hezekiah saw - This was in the fourteenth year of the reign of Hezekiah; and at first the Jewish king bought him off at the great price of three hundred talents of silver, and thirty talents of gold; and even emptied his own treasures, and spoiled the house of the Lord, to gratify the oppressive avarice of the Assyrian king. See the whole account, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.13">2Kgs 18:13</reference>, etc.
entries.2fa00407ee09d74133bb64fae2518ba9d1694aae: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen14574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14575" type="x-p"/> Stopped all the fountains - This was prudently done, for without water how could an immense army subsist in an arid country? No doubt the Assyrian army suffered much through this, as a Christian army did eighteen hundred years after this. When the crusaders came, in a.d. 1099, to besiege Jerusalem, the people of the city stopped up the wells, so that the Christian army was reduced to the greatest necessities and distress.
entries.978098f48b038892ee87291e9042604f685f6a97: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen14575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14576" type="x-p"/> Raised it up to the towers - He built the wall up to the height of the towers, or, having built the wall, he raised towers on it.
entries.580a5c0778d494d22fc9a79c98e9bc8507598c51: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen14576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14577" type="x-p"/> Set captains of war over the people - in the street of the gate of the city - That is, the open places at the gate of the city, whither the people came for judgment, etc.
entries.00dde1ae68f89640c2644e0b08fcb5b0a349d350: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen14577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14578" type="x-p"/> There be more with us than with him - We have more power than they have. (These words he quotes from the prophet Elisha, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.16">2Kgs 6:16</reference>). This was soon proved to be true by the slaughter made by the angel of the Lord in the Assyrian camp.
entries.dfe8578671763b20f2fda40c147b6cd84cc54de9: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen14578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14579" type="x-p"/> After this did Sennacherib - Having received the silver and gold mentioned above, he withdrew his army, but shortly after he sent Rab-shakeh with a blasphemous message. This is the fact mentioned here.
entries.40a522046905e3513a3837dd4d577d1e39d2c9d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen14579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14580" type="x-p"/> Thus saith Sennacherib - See all these circumstances largely explained 2 Kings 18:17-36 (note).
entries.98deaf981feedb6a9982b5321f29b9190df1bd02: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen14580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14581" type="x-p"/> Wrote also letters - See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.9">2Kgs 19:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.14">2Kgs 19:14</reference>.
entries.6806f186754e6622d48121e3cb1d179df2b37fb3: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen14581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14582" type="x-p"/> The Lord sent an angel - See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.36">2Kgs 19:36</reference> (note), and the note there. <div eID="gen14582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14583" type="x-p"/> House of his god - Nisroch. <div eID="gen14583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14584" type="x-p"/> They that came forth of his own bowels - His sons Adrammelech and Sharezer.
entries.34ad6528feb6fc5a004ce4b78505ffa8043a9dad: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen14584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14585" type="x-p"/> Many brought gifts unto the Lord - They plainly saw that Jehovah was the protector of the land. <div eID="gen14585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14586" type="x-p"/> And presents to Hezekiah - They saw that God was his friend, and would undertake for him; and they did not wish to have such a man for their enemy.
entries.10e5c31c57a451cb57643387cbc0d95cf6ff1a03: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen14586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14587" type="x-p"/> Hezekiah was sick - See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.1">2Kgs 20:1</reference> (note), etc., and the notes there.
entries.9f48ba5ade3280ff7037f0ee2599da78073307ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen14587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14588" type="x-p"/> Hezekiah rendered not again - He got into a vain confidence, took pleasure in his riches, and vainly showed them to the messengers of the king of Babylon. See on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.12">2Kgs 20:12</reference> (note), etc.
entries.38d365b29d2b36cdbcfc756eb7284981dea52aa5: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen14588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14589" type="x-p"/> Humbled himself - Awoke from his sleep, was sorry for his sin, deprecated the wrath of God, and the Divine displeasure was turned away from him.
entries.19d0bcbdd883fef24271e84743e260aee9bfce09: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen14589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14590" type="x-p"/> Pleasant jewels - כלי חמדה keley chemdah, desirable vessels or utensils.
entries.2470e360a43879389e173c932040fa6f8c33ae2d: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen14590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14591" type="x-p"/> The upper watercourse - He made canals to bring the waters of Gihon from the west side of Jerusalem to the west side of the city of David.
entries.c7414648787e3d1c8019ff77c7694336873f4eef: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen14591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14592" type="x-p"/> Of the ambassadors - See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.13">2Kgs 20:13</reference> (note), and the observations at the end of that chapter.
entries.2ac63d097a2cbcbbafc22e559398b9e98787a8f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen14592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14593" type="x-p"/> The vision of Isaiah - See this prophet, 2 Chronicles 36-39.
entries.f2aae6c50fb4318e91402d4c487aa997061d9c80: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen14593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14594" type="x-p"/> Chiefest of the sepulchres - This respect they paid to him who, since David, had been the best of all their kings. <div eID="gen14594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14595" type="x-p"/> I shall subjoin a few things from the Targum on this chapter. <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.1">2Chr 32:1</reference>. "After these things which Hezekiah did, and their establishment, the Lord appointed by his Word to bring Sennacherib, king of Assyria, and his army, into the land of Israel, that he might destroy the Assyrians in the land of the house of Judah, and smite their troops on the mountains of Jerusalem, and deliver all their spoils into the hands of Hezekiah and his people: wherefore Sennacherib came with immense armies, which could not be numbered; and having pitched his camps in the land of the tribe of Judah, besieged their fortified cities with his armies, hoping to overthrow them." <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.8">2Chr 32:8</reference>. Hezekiah said-"His help is the strength of the flesh; but our auxiliary is the Word of the Lord." <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.16">2Chr 32:16</reference>. "His (Sennacherib's) servants spoke blasphemy against the Word of the Lord God." <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.18">2Chr 32:18</reference>. In the Jews' speech - "In the language of the holy house." <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.21">2Chr 32:21</reference>. "And the Word of the Lord sent Michael, and the angel Gabriel, and destroyed them on the night of the passover with a destructive fire; and burnt up their breath within their bodies, and consumed every soldier, captain, and prince, in the army of the king of Assyria; and he returned with shame of face into his own land." <div eID="gen14595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14596" type="x-p"/> The destruction of God's enemies, and the support and salvation of the faithful, is in every instance in this Targum attributed to the Word of the Lord, personally understood. See the note on <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.27">2Chr 34:27</reference>. <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.24">2Chr 32:24</reference>. "In those days was Hezekiah sick near to death; but he prayed before the Lord who spoke to him by his Word to preserve him and to add to his life fifteen years." <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.31">2Chr 32:31</reference>. "The king of Babylon sent, that they might inquire concerning the miracle that had been done in the land; that they might see the two tables of stone which were in the ark of the covenant of the Lord which Moses had placed there with the two tables which he had broken on account of the sin of the calf which they made in Horeb. The Word of the Lord permitted him to show them these; neither did he suffer for it; that he might try him, and see what was in his heart." <div eID="gen14596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14597" type="x-p"/> Thus God speaks after the manner of men: he either brings, or permits them to be brought, into such circumstances as shall cause them to show their prevailing propensities; and then warns them against the evils to which they are inclined, after having shown them that they are capable of those evils. To know ourselves, and our own character, is of the utmost importance to our religious growth and perfection. He who does not know where his weakness lies, is not likely to know where his strength lies. Many, by not being fully acquainted with their own character, have been unwatchful and unguarded, and so become an easy prey to their enemies. Know thyself is a lesson which no man can learn but from the Spirit of God.  <chapter eID="2Chr.32"/> <div eID="gen14597" type="x-p"/>

entries.7865de6cb8d84b2eb2e2c4e1002eda4dc50dfb59: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.1">2Ch 32:1</reference> <div eID="gen6205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6206" type="x-p"/> The didactic and rhetorical character of the narrative is manifest in the very form of the introductory statement. Instead of the chronological statement of 2Ki 18:13, we find the loose formula of connection: after these events and this fidelity (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.20">2Ch 31:20</reference>), Sennacherib came (בּא) and entered into Judah (ביהוּדה ויּבא), and besieged the fenced cities, and thought (ויּאמר) to break (conquer) them for himself. He had already taken a number of them, and had advanced as far as Lachish in the south-west of Judah, when he made the attempt to get Jerusalem into his power; cf. 2Ki 18:13.
entries.65ed7ffd2f447057fed4802b666174b5708e14e2: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.2-2Chr.32.8">2Ch 32:2-8</reference> <hi type="italic">Preparations of Hezekiah for the strengthening and defending of Jerusalem</hi>. - We find an account of this neither in 2 Kings 18 nor in Isa 36; ; but the fact is confirmed both by <reference osisRef="Isa.22.8-Isa.22.11">Isa 22:8-11</reference>, and by the remark 2Ki 20:20 (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.30">2Ch 32:30</reference> of our chapter).  <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.2-2Chr.32.4">2Ch 32:2-4</reference> <div eID="gen6206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6207" type="x-p"/> When Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib advanced, and his face was to war against Jerusalem, i.e., that he purposed to capture Jerusalem, he consulted with his princes and his valiant men to cover the waters of the springs which were outside the city; and they helped him, brought much people together, and covered all the springs, and the brook which ran through the midst of the land. סתם does not denote to obstruct, but only to hide by covering and conducting the water into subterranean channels. The brook which flowed through the midst of the land is the Gihon, which was formed by the waters flowing from the springs, and was dried up by these springs being covered and the water diverted. For further information, see on 2Ch 32:30. The object of this measure is stated in the words which follow: Why should the kings of Assyria come and find much water? i.e., why should we provide them with much water, when they advance against the city and besiege it? The plural, kings of Assyria, is rhetorical, as in 2Ch 28:16.
entries.e12990faecc8965ea428dee653a837ee089d8998: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.9">2Ch 32:9</reference> <hi type="italic">The advance of an Assyrian army against Jerusalem</hi>, and the attempts of Sennacherib’s generals to induce the population of the capital to submit by persuasive and threatening speeches, are very breifly narrated, in comparison with 2 Kings 18:17-36. In <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.9">2Ch 32:9</reference>, neither the names of the Assyrian generals, nor the names of Hezekiah’s ambassadors with whom they treated, are given; nor is the place where the negotiation was carried on mentioned. עבדיו, his servants, Sennacherib’s generals. על־לך, while he himself lay near (or against) Lachish, and all the army of his kingdom with him. ממשׁלתּו, his dominion, i.e., army of his kingdom; cf. Jer 34:1.
entries.0fe06538803b1a6998f3eb43383895bbcdf13437: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.10-2Chr.32.12">2Ch 32:10-12</reference> <div eID="gen6209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6210" type="x-p"/> Only the main ideas contained in the speech of these generals are reported; in <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.10-2Chr.32.12">2Ch 32:10-12</reference> we have the attempt to shake the trust of the people in Hezekiah and in God (2Ki 18:19-22). וישׁבים is a continuation of the question, In what do ye trust, and why sit ye in the distress, in Jerusalem? מסּית as in 2Ki 18:32 : Hezekiah seduces you, to give you over to death by hunger and thirst. This thought is much more coarsely expressed in 2Ki 18:27. - On <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.12">2Ch 32:12</reference>, cf. 2Ki 18:22 : אחד מזבּח is the one altar of burnt-offering in the temple.
entries.b21d6ddb3f51e2aecd5bd0afc55a0a9d01e06a34: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.13-2Chr.32.19">2Ch 32:13-19</reference> <div eID="gen6210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6211" type="x-p"/> The description of Sennacherib’s all-conquering power: cf. 2Ki 18:35; <reference osisRef="Isa.36.20">Isa 36:20</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.37.11">Isa 37:11</reference>-13. “Who is there among all the gods of these peoples, whom my fathers utterly destroyed, who could have delivered his people out of my hand, that your God should save you?” The idea is, that since the gods of the other peoples, which were mightier than your God, have not been able to save their peoples, how should your God be in a position to rescue you from my power? This idea is again repeated in <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.15">2Ch 32:15</reference>, as a foundation for the exhortation not to let themselves be deceived and misled by Hezekiah, and not to believe his words, and that in an assertative form: “for not one god of any nation or kingdom was able to deliver his people, ... much less then (כּי אף) your gods: they will not save you;” and this is done in order to emphasize strongly the blasphemy of the Assyrian generals against the Almighty God of Israel. To communicate more of these blasphemous speeches would in the chronicler’s view be useless, and he therefore only remarks, in <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.16">2Ch 32:16</reference>, “And yet more spake his (Sennacherib’s) servants against God Jahve, and against His servant Hezekiah;” and then, in <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.17">2Ch 32:17</reference>, that Sennacherib also wrote a letter of similar purport, and (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.18">2Ch 32:18</reference>) that his servants called with a loud voice in the Jews’ speech to the people of Jerusalem upon the wall, to throw them into fear and terrify them, that they might take the city. What they called to the people is not stated, but by the infinit. וּלבהלם ליראם it is hinted, and thence we may gather that it was to the same effect as the blasphemous speeches above quoted (יראם, inf. Pi., as in <reference osisRef="Neh.6.19">Neh 6:19</reference>). - On comparing 2 Kings 18 and 19, it is clear that Sennacherib only sent the letter to Hezekiah after his general Rabshakeh had informed him of the fruitlessness of his efforts to induce the people of Jerusalem to submit by speeches, and the news of the advance of the Cushite king Tirhakah had arrived; while the calling aloud in the Jews’ language to the people standing on the wall, on the part of his generals, took place in the first negotiation with the ambassadors of Hezekiah. The author of the Chronicle has arranged his narrative rhetorically, so as to make the various events form a climax: first, the speeches of the servants of Sennacherib; then the king’s letter to Hezekiah to induce him and his counsellors to submit; and finally, the attempt to terrify the people in language intelligible to them. The conclusion is the statement, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.19">2Ch 32:19</reference> : “They spake of the God of Jerusalem as of the gods of the peoples of the earth, the work of the hands of man;” cf. 2Ki 19:18.
entries.977920faf813a7e87ef33c167f5698ce243b5b66: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.20">2Ch 32:20</reference> <hi type="italic">Prayer of King Hezekiah and of the prophet Isaiah for the help of the Lord</hi>. - 2Ch 32:20. The main contents of Hezekiah’s prayer are communicated in 2Ki 19:14-19 and <reference osisRef="Isa.37.15">Isa 37:15</reference>-19. There it is not expressly said that Isaiah also prayed, but it may be inferred from the statement in 2Ki 19:2. and Isa 37:2. that Hezekiah sent a deputation to the prophet with the request that he would pray for the people. In answer Isaiah promised the ambassadors deliverance, as the word of the Lord. זאת על, on account of this, i.e., on account of the contempt shown for the God of Israel, which was emphatically dwelt upon both in the prayer of Hezekiah (2Ki 19:16) and in the word of Isaiah, v. 22ff.
entries.9d64a3aec9e77cc121af00ec3f38bc6fb92abf46: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.21">2Ch 32:21</reference> <div eID="gen6211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6212" type="x-p"/> The deliverance: cf. 2Ki 19:35.; Isa 37:36. The number of Assyrians smitten by the angel of the Lord is not stated, as it was not of importance, the main fact being that the whole Assyrian host was annihilated, so that Sennacherib had to return with disgrace into his own land. This is what is signified by the rhetorical phrase: The angel of Jahve destroyed all the valiant warriors, and the leaders and princes of the king of Assyria, and he returned with shame of face (cf. Ezr 9:7; <reference osisRef="Ps.44.16">Psa 44:16</reference>) to his land, where his sons slew him in the temple. In regard to the facts, see on 2Ki 19:37 and Isa 37:38. The Keth. מיציאו is an orthographical error for מיציאי, a contraction of מן and יציאי from יציא, a passive formation with intransitive signification: some of those who went forth from his own bowels, i.e., some of his sons; cf. the similar formation miyliydeey, 1Ch 20:4.
entries.8e38d0bd7a95a19f0bbb0230882745ccf3229312: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.22">2Ch 32:22</reference> <div eID="gen6212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6213" type="x-p"/> Conclusion of this event. So the Lord helped, etc., מיּד־כּל, and out of the hand of all, sc. his enemies; but we need not on that account, with some manuscripts, bring איביו into the text. וינהלם, and protected them round about. נהל, to lead, guide, with the additional idea of care and protection (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.4">Psa 31:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.10">Isa 49:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.18">Isa 51:18</reference>); and consequently here, protect, defend. There is therefore no need of the conjecture להם ויּנח להם erut, which Berth. holds to be the original reading, without considering that, though מסּביב ויּנח is a current phrase with the chronicler (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.6">2Ch 14:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.15">2Ch 15:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.30">2Ch 20:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.18">1Ch 22:18</reference>), the supposition that these words became וינהלם מס by an orthographical error is not at all probable.
entries.98c976103c148caa3420554114e4bfba5ec5e6df: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.23">2Ch 32:23</reference> <div eID="gen6213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6214" type="x-p"/> Many brought gifts to the Lord to Jerusalem, and presents to King Hezekiah. רבּים is not to be restricted to Israelites, but probably denotes chiefly neighbouring peoples, who by the destruction of the Assyrian army were also freed from this dreaded enemy. They, too, might feel impelled to show their reverence for the God of Israel, who had so wonderfully delivered His people by their gifts.
entries.bd3d15b4ff59bbc38804102d2bcd922f541de6d7: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.24">2Ch 32:24</reference> <hi type="italic">Hezekiah’s sickness and recovery; his pride and his humiliation</hi>. - 2Ch 32:24. As to the sickness of Hezekiah, and the miraculous sign by which the prophet Isaiah assured him of recovery, see the account in 2Ki 20:1-11 and Isa 38. The Chronicle has only given us hints on this matter. ויּאמר and נתן refer to the same subject - God. Hezekiah prayed, and in consequence of his prayer God spake to him, sc. by the mouth of the prophet, and gave him a miraculous sign.
entries.ada74b1e88ee2b6d0d3e06f028da40795fefc63f: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.25">2Ch 32:25</reference> “But Hezekiah rendered not according to the benefit unto him, for his heart was proud.” In his sickness he had promised to walk in humility all his days (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.15">Isa 38:15</reference>): yet he became proud after his recovery; and his pride showed itself especially in his showing all his treasures to the Babylonian embassy, in idle trust in them and in the resources at his command (cf. 2Ki 20:12-15; <reference osisRef="Isa.39.1-Isa.39.4">Isa 39:1-4</reference>). “And there was wrath upon him, and upon Judah and Jerusalem,” which participated in the king’s sentiments (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.10">2Ch 19:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.24">1Ch 27:24</reference>). Isaiah proclaimed this wrath to him in the prophecy that all the treasures of the king would be carried away to Babylon, and that some of his sons should become courtiers of the king of Babylon (2Ki 20:16-18; <reference osisRef="Isa.39.5-Isa.39.7">Isa 39:5-7</reference>), to which we should perhaps also reckon the threatening prophecy in Mic 3:12.
entries.b5a5a4745edcdf0d29b957870da21ba35997ddd7: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.26">2Ch 32:26</reference> <div eID="gen6214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6215" type="x-p"/> Then Hezekiah humbled himself in his pride, and the wrath came not upon them in the days of Hezekiah (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.39.8">Isa 39:8</reference>). The threatened judgment was postponed because of this humiliation, and broke over the royal house and the whole kingdom only at a later time in the Chaldean invasion.
entries.126a5cfa4452db85f1e1aaf2566b66d9370ffc4c: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.27">2Ch 32:27</reference> <hi type="italic">Hezekiah’s riches; concluding estimate of his reign; his death and burial</hi>. - 2Ch 32:27. Like Jehoshaphat (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.5">2Ch 17:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.1">2Ch 18:1</reference>), Solomon (<reference osisRef="2Chr.1.12">2Ch 1:12</reference>), and David (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.28">1Ch 29:28</reference>), Hezekiah attained to riches and glory, and made unto himself treasure-chambers for silver, gold, precious stones, and spices, shields, and all manner of splendid furniture. The מגנּים are named instead of weapons in general. The collection of them brings to recollection the כּליו בּית   (2Ki 20:13 and <reference osisRef="Isa.39.2">Isa 39:2</reference>).
entries.5097476333ff7c6bbe4cae7a6b4838f2117a372e: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.28">2Ch 32:28</reference> <div eID="gen6215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6216" type="x-p"/> Storehouses also (magazines) for the agricultural produce, and stalls for all manner of cattle, and stalls for the herds, like David (1Ch 27:25.) and Uzziah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.10">2Ch 26:10</reference>). מסכּנות is a transposition of מכנסות, storehouses, from כּנס, to heap up. “Cattle and cattle” = all kinds of cattle. ארות, synonymous with אריות   (<reference osisRef="2Chr.9.5">2Ch 9:5</reference>), stables or stalls for cattle. The word אורות, which occurs only here, must have the same signification, and be held to be a transposed form of that word.
entries.bb00aa51d421e35eb0329bbe5298bc0dd8f728d0: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.29">2Ch 32:29</reference> <div eID="gen6216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6217" type="x-p"/> And cities (?) made (procured) he for himself. ערים cannot in this connection denote the usual cities; it must mean either watch-towers (from עוּר, to watch) or dwelling-places for herds and cattle, since עיר, according to 2Ki 17:9, is used of any enclosed place, from a watch-tower to a fenced city. רכוּשׁ, as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.3">2Ch 31:3</reference>, of possessions in herds.
entries.2ce92732ac1277af2a039bf1eb9abac4b4541c4e: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.30">2Ch 32:30</reference> <div eID="gen6217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6218" type="x-p"/> The same Hezekiah covered the upper outlet of the water Gihon, and brought it down westwards to the city of David, i.e., by a subterranean channel into the city of David (see on <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.3">2Ch 32:3</reference>). The form ויישׁרם is Piel ויישּׁרם; the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> is the same conjug., only contracted into ויּשּׁרם, as ויּבּשׁ for וייבּשׁ, the ו of the third person having amalgamated with the first radical, under the influence of the ו <hi type="italic">consec</hi>. With the last clause in <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.30">2Ch 32:30</reference> cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.21">2Ch 31:21</reference>; 1Ch 29:23.
entries.0068280588bf9bd057326e24381347151fc0aad7: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.31">2Ch 32:31</reference> “And so (i.e., accordingly) in the case of the ambassadors of the princes of Babylon, ... God left him.” וכן does not denote <hi type="italic">attamen</hi>; it never has an adversative meaning. Bertheau rightly translates, “and accordingly,” with the further remark, that by וכן the account of Hezekiah’s treatment of the Babylonian ambassadors, which could not be reckoned among his fortunate deeds, is brought into harmony with the remark that he prospered in all his undertakings. It was permitted by God that Hezekiah should on this occasion be lifted up, and should commit an iniquity which could not but bring misfortune with it; not in order that He might plunge him into misfortune, but to try him, and to humble him (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.26">2Ch 32:26</reference>).
entries.24f1036ff9930944fa97d58e97a54d70ec5f2c1e: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.32">2Ch 32:32</reference> הסדים, pious deeds, as in 2Ch 6:42. ישׂ הזון is the book of Isaiah’s prophecies; see the Introduction.
entries.873ec459f905785ef982b9c87dc01d60f30f6bbe: <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.33">2Ch 32:33</reference> <div eID="gen6218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6219" type="x-p"/> Hezekiah was buried “on the height of the graves of the sons of David,” perhaps because there was no longer room in the hereditary burying-place of the kings; so that for Hezekiah and the succeeding kings special graves had to be prepared in a higher place of the graves of the kings. “They did him honour in his death,” by the burning of many spices, as we may conjecture (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.14">2Ch 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.19">2Ch 21:19</reference>).  <chapter eID="2Chr.32"/> <div eID="gen6219" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="12">12 Hath not the same Hezekiah taken away his high places, and his altars, and commanded Judah and Jerusalem, saying, Ye shall worship before one altar, and burn incense upon it?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Know ye not what I and my fathers have done unto all the people of <ns0:hi>other</ns0:hi> lands? were the gods of the nations of those lands any ways able to deliver their lands out of mine hand?</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="25">25 But Hezekiah rendred not again, according to the benefit <ns0:hi>done</ns0:hi> unto him: for his heart was lift<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed up <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">For that prodigious Victory over the Assyrians, above <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 21. and for his miraculous Restauration from Sickness, and the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />firmation of that Work by a strange and supernatural Motion of the Sun; and by the Honour since done him by an Embassy from the great and potent King of Babylon.
